prompt: What does server side rendering (SSR) mean?

options.text: The page HTML is built on the server for every request
options.why: Each visitor causes the server to build the page again. That is how the page can show something different for each person, or data that changed a second ago.

options.text: The page HTML is built once when you deploy
options.why: That is static generation (SSG). It builds one copy and serves the same HTML to everyone.

options.text: The page is built in the browser by JavaScript
options.why: That is client side rendering (CSR). The server sends an almost empty page and JavaScript fills it in.

options.text: The page is rebuilt on a timer after it is deployed
options.why: That is incremental static regeneration (ISR), a static page that refreshes itself every so often.

hint: The name says where the work happens. When does it happen?

prompt: What does static site generation (SSG) mean?

options.text: The HTML is built once at build time and reused
options.why: The work happens before anybody visits. Every visitor then gets the same ready-made file, which is why it is the fastest option.

options.text: The HTML is built fresh for every visitor
options.why: That is SSR. SSG does the work once, not once per request.

options.text: The page cannot use JavaScript at all
options.why: "Static" describes when the HTML was made, not whether the page is interactive. A static page can still run JavaScript.

options.text: The page is stored only in the browser cache
options.why: The built HTML lives on the server or a CDN. A browser cache is a separate thing on top.

hint: How many times is the HTML built?

prompt: What is incremental static regeneration (ISR)?

options.text: A static page that rebuilds itself after a set time
options.why: You get the speed of a static page, but it refreshes in the background every so often, so the data does not go stale forever.

options.text: A page rebuilt on every single request
options.why: That is SSR. ISR rebuilds on a timer, not per request, which is why it stays fast.

options.text: A page that is never rebuilt after deploy
options.why: That is plain SSG. The whole point of ISR is that it does rebuild.

options.text: A page rendered only in the browser
options.why: That is CSR. ISR produces real HTML on the server.

hint: It is static, plus one extra ability.

prompt: A page shows each user their own account balance, which must always be current. Which rendering strategy fits?

options.text: SSR
options.why: The content differs per user and must be fresh, so it has to be built per request. Nothing built ahead of time can know who is asking.

options.text: SSG
options.why: A page built once at deploy would show every user the same numbers, and they would be out of date.

options.text: ISR
options.why: ISR still serves one shared page, just refreshed on a timer. It cannot show a different balance per user.

options.text: It does not matter, they all give the same result
options.why: They differ in WHEN the HTML is built, and that decides whether it can be personal and fresh.

hint: Can a page built before you arrived know who you are?

prompt: A blog post never changes once published and is the same for everybody. Which strategy is the best fit?

options.text: SSG
options.why: Same for everyone and rarely changing is exactly the case for building once. The page is then served as a plain file, which is the fastest thing a server can do.

options.text: SSR
options.why: Rebuilding identical HTML for every visitor is wasted work and makes the page slower for no gain.

options.text: CSR
options.why: Rendering in the browser delays the text and hides it from search engines, which is bad for a blog.

options.text: ISR
options.why: ISR is for content that changes sometimes. If the post never changes there is nothing to regenerate.

hint: If the answer is the same for everyone forever, why build it twice?

prompt: In the older Pages Router, which function makes a page server side rendered?

options.text: getServerSideProps
options.why: The name says it: it fetches props on the server, for every request. Next.js sees the export and switches that page to SSR.

options.text: getStaticProps
options.why: That one runs at BUILD time and makes the page static, which is SSG.

options.text: getStaticPaths
options.why: That lists which dynamic pages to build ahead of time. It picks the addresses, not the rendering mode.

options.text: getInitialProps
options.why: That is the oldest API of the three and is no longer recommended. It can run in either place, which is part of why it was replaced.

hint: Read the names literally. Which says "server side"?

prompt: In the older Pages Router, which function makes a page statically generated?

options.text: getStaticProps
options.why: It runs once at build time and hands the result to the page as props, so the HTML is made before anybody visits.

options.text: getServerSideProps
options.why: That runs on every request, which is SSR, the opposite of static.

options.text: useEffect
options.why: That is a React hook that runs in the BROWSER after the page shows. It cannot build HTML on the server.

options.text: generateStaticParams
options.why: That is the App Router name, and it lists which dynamic pages to build rather than fetching the data for one.

hint: Static means built at build time.

prompt: In the App Router, what is a component by default?

options.text: A server component
options.why: Server is the default, which is the big change from the old router. You have to opt OUT to get a client component.

options.text: A client component
options.why: That was effectively the old default. In the App Router you must ask for it with "use client".

options.text: Both, Next.js decides automatically
options.why: Next.js does not guess. The boundary is set by you, with the "use client" directive.

options.text: Neither until you add a directive
options.why: A component with no directive still works. It is simply a server component.

hint: Which one needs you to write something extra?

prompt: What does putting "use client" at the top of a file do?

options.text: It marks the file and what it imports as client components
options.why: It sets the boundary where server rendering stops and the browser takes over. Everything imported below that point is bundled for the browser too.

options.text: It stops the component rendering on the server at all
options.why: A client component is still pre-rendered to HTML on the server. The directive decides where it becomes interactive, not whether it is rendered.

options.text: It makes the page client side rendered only
options.why: It applies to that component, not to the whole page. A page can mix server and client components.

options.text: It turns off JavaScript for that file
options.why: The opposite. It is how you get JavaScript shipped to the browser for that component.

hint: It is a boundary marker, not an on/off switch.

prompt: Which of these forces a component to be a client component?

options.text: Using useState or an onClick handler
options.why: State and event handlers only exist in the browser. A server component is rendered once and sent as HTML, so it has nowhere to keep state or receive a click.

options.text: Reading from a database
options.why: That is the opposite. Touching a database is a reason to STAY on the server, where the credentials are safe.

options.text: Using async and await
options.why: A server component can be an async function. That is one of the things the App Router added.

options.text: Importing a CSS file
options.why: Styles work in both. Importing CSS does not move a component to the browser.

hint: What does a component need a live browser for?

prompt: Which of these can a server component NOT do?

options.text: Respond to a button click with useState
options.why: A server component runs once, on the server, and sends HTML. It is gone by the time the user clicks, so it has no state and no event handlers.

options.text: Fetch data with await before rendering
options.why: It can. A server component may be an async function and await its data directly, with no useEffect needed.

options.text: Read a secret API key from the environment
options.why: It can, and this is a main reason to use one. The key never reaches the browser.

options.text: Render another component
options.why: It can render both server and client components inside it.

hint: What has already finished by the time the user sees the page?

prompt: What is a main benefit of a server component?

options.text: Its code is never sent to the browser, so less is downloaded
options.why: The component runs on the server and only the finished HTML travels. A heavy library used there adds nothing to what the user downloads.

options.text: It makes the page interactive without JavaScript
options.why: Interactivity is exactly what it cannot do. That is what client components are for.

options.text: It removes the need for a server
options.why: The name says the opposite. It needs a server to run on.

options.text: It makes CSS load faster
options.why: Styles are handled the same way either side of the boundary.

hint: Think about what is NOT downloaded.

prompt: In the App Router, which file name makes a route show a page?

options.text: page.tsx
options.why: A folder only becomes a visitable route when it holds a page file. The folder name is the address and page.tsx is what is shown.

options.text: index.tsx
options.why: That is the Pages Router convention. The App Router replaced it with page.tsx.

options.text: route.tsx
options.why: route.ts is for an API endpoint that returns data, not a page for a person to look at.

options.text: layout.tsx
options.why: A layout wraps pages with shared chrome such as a nav bar. On its own it shows no route.

hint: The App Router names files after what they are.

prompt: What is layout.tsx for in the App Router?

options.text: Shared UI that wraps every page below it and keeps its state when you navigate
options.why: A layout holds the parts that should not flash or reset, such as a sidebar or a nav bar. Moving between pages inside it does not rebuild it.

options.text: The page shown at that address
options.why: That is page.tsx. A layout only wraps.

options.text: The loading spinner shown while a page fetches
options.why: That is loading.tsx, a separate convention.

options.text: The 404 page for that folder
options.why: That is not-found.tsx.

hint: What should NOT reset when you move between pages?

prompt: In the App Router, how do you make a route that matches /blog/anything?

options.text: A folder named [slug] inside blog
options.why: Square brackets mark a part of the address that varies. The name inside the brackets becomes the parameter you read in the page.

options.text: A folder named {slug} inside blog
options.why: Curly braces are JavaScript syntax. Next.js routing uses square brackets.

options.text: A folder named :slug inside blog
options.why: A leading colon is the Express and React Router style. Next.js uses the folder name itself.

options.text: A file named blog/*.tsx
options.why: A star is not a routing convention in Next.js, and a route needs a folder with page.tsx.

hint: Look at the brackets, not the name.

prompt: What does adding loading.tsx to a folder do?

options.text: Shows that UI automatically while the page is fetching
options.why: Next.js wraps the page so the fallback appears straight away and the real content swaps in when it is ready. You write no state for it.

options.text: Makes the page load faster
options.why: It changes what the user SEES while waiting. The data takes just as long.

options.text: Runs code before the page loads
options.why: That is closer to middleware. loading.tsx is only what is displayed.

options.text: Preloads the next page
options.why: Next.js prefetches links on its own. That is not what this file does.

hint: The file name is what the user sees, not what the code does.

prompt: Why use the Link component instead of a plain <a> tag in Next.js?

options.text: It moves between pages without a full reload, and prefetches them
options.why: Only the changed part of the page is replaced, so state is kept and the move feels instant. Next.js also fetches the target ahead of time.

options.text: A plain <a> tag does not work at all in Next.js
options.why: It works and still navigates. You just lose the speed and the kept state.

options.text: Link is required for external websites
options.why: The opposite. For another site a plain <a> is the right choice, since there is nothing to prefetch.

options.text: Link adds styling to the link
options.why: It adds no styles. You style it yourself.

hint: What happens to the rest of the page when you click?

prompt: What does { next: { revalidate: 60 } } on a fetch mean?

options.text: The cached result may be reused for 60 seconds, then refreshed
options.why: This is ISR at the level of one fetch. Within the window everyone gets the stored copy; after it, the next request triggers a refresh.

options.text: The fetch times out after 60 seconds
options.why: revalidate is about how long the ANSWER stays usable, not how long to wait for it.

options.text: The fetch is retried every 60 seconds forever
options.why: Nothing refetches on its own in the background with no traffic. A request after the window is what triggers it.

options.text: The page is rebuilt 60 times
options.why: 60 is a number of seconds, not a count.

hint: Sixty what, and of what?

prompt: What does { cache: "no-store" } on a fetch do?

options.text: Fetches fresh data on every request, never reusing a cached copy
options.why: This is how you opt a server component into true SSR behaviour: the data, and so the page, is rebuilt for each visitor.

options.text: Stores the result in the browser instead of the server
options.why: "no-store" means do not store anywhere. It is not a choice of where.

options.text: Clears the whole cache
options.why: It affects this one fetch, not everything cached elsewhere.

options.text: Makes the fetch run in the browser
options.why: It changes caching only. Where the fetch runs is decided by whether the component is a server or client one.

hint: Read it literally: do not store.

prompt: What is a Server Action in Next.js?

options.text: A function marked "use server" that the browser can call, but which runs on the server
options.why: It lets a form or a button trigger server code directly, so you do not have to hand-write an API endpoint and a fetch to reach it.

options.text: A component that renders only on the server
options.why: That is a server component. An action is a function you call, not something that renders.

options.text: A background job that runs on a schedule
options.why: Nothing in Next.js schedules it. It runs because something in the browser called it.

options.text: Middleware that runs before every request
options.why: That is middleware.ts, a separate feature.

hint: "use client" marks a boundary one way. What does "use server" mark?

prompt: Which environment variable is sent to the browser in a Next.js app?

options.text: One whose name starts with NEXT_PUBLIC_
options.why: The prefix is the opt-in. Anything without it stays on the server, which is what keeps secret keys out of the bundle.

options.text: Every variable in .env
options.why: That would leak every secret you own into the browser. The prefix exists precisely to stop it.

options.text: Only ones used inside a client component
options.why: Where you use it does not matter. A variable without the prefix is simply undefined in the browser.

options.text: None, they are always server only
options.why: Some values do need to reach the browser, such as a public API address. The prefix is how you allow it.

hint: The rule is in the NAME of the variable.

prompt: In the App Router, how do you set a page title?

options.text: Export a metadata object from the page or layout
options.why: Next.js reads the exported object and writes the head tags for you, so you never touch <head> yourself.

options.text: Put a <title> tag in your JSX
options.why: The App Router manages the head. Writing the tag by hand is the old way and can be overwritten.

options.text: Use the next/head component
options.why: next/head is the Pages Router tool. The App Router replaced it with the metadata export.

options.text: Set it in next.config.js
options.why: That file configures the build, not the content of one page.

hint: The App Router prefers exports over tags.

prompt: What is the main drawback of rendering a page entirely in the browser (CSR)?

options.text: The user and search engines see an empty page until the JavaScript runs
options.why: The server sends almost nothing, so there is a blank gap while the bundle downloads and runs. That hurts both the first impression and search ranking.

options.text: It cannot fetch data
options.why: It fetches fine. The problem is WHEN, not whether.

options.text: It does not work on mobile
options.why: It works everywhere. It is just slower to first paint, which is felt most on a slow phone.

options.text: It needs a more powerful server
options.why: The opposite. The server does less work, because the browser does it all.

hint: What is on screen during the wait?
